paper_title: $λ_0$: Scaling Open-World Egocentric Human Data for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated whole-body interaction with the physical world, yet collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains costly. Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but existing egocentric human supervision often omits locomotion and posture, while embodiment differences and controller dynamics hinder accurate end-effector execution. We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion. Our human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, and refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while preserving whole-body coordination. We validate the pipeline through zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations. Building on this pipeline, we develop $λ_0$, a humanoid foundation model for whole-body loco-manipulation, with robot-aligned human demonstrations providing supervision for mid-training. Increasing whole-body human data consistently improves downstream task progress. $λ_0$ achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks. We expect this study to guide scalable whole-body human data collection toward humanoid foundation models for richer interaction with the physical world. Homepage: https://lambdahumanoid.github.io/

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Learning humanoid loco-manipulation across tasks and environments requires demonstrations that capture coordinated locomotion, posture, and manipulation (Jiang et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026b; Hu et al., 2026; Figure AI, 2026a;b). Whole-body teleoperation provides visual observations paired with robot actions, but requires operators to guide physical humanoid through each demonstration (Fu et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026b; GEAR Team et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b). This dependence on robot availability and operation makes broader task and environment coverage costly to obtain (Shi et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026). Scaling humanoid learning motivates source of whole-body interaction experience that can grow beyond robot-operated collection. Egocentric video records peoples everyday interactions across tasks and environments without requiring robot operation (Grauman et al., 2022; Kareer et al., 2025; Hoque et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026; Figure, 2026). Recent methods recover wrist and hand trajectories from these videos, turning observed interactions into action supervision for robot learning (Li et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a). Pretraining on these action-labeled videos can improve downstream manipulation (Zheng et al., 2026c; Punamiya et al., 2026). For humanoid loco-manipulation, however, wrist and hand trajectories alone omit the locomotion and postural changes that support whole-body interaction (Shi et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a). Recording synchronized body and hand motion captures this coordination, but motion retargeting and whole-body tracking can still leave end-effector errors due to geometric mismatch and imperfect execution (Araujo et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026b). These errors can compromise grasping and contact. This raises our central question: Can egocentric whole-body human experience provide supervision that is both transferable to humanoids and practical to acquire at scale? We develop human-to-humanoid alignment pipeline that captures human demonstrations without robot and aligns their observations and actions to the downstream humanoid (Sec. 3.4). We match the camera and capture height to the robot setup, then remove human forearms and trackers from the images and composite rendered G1 arms. Action alignment refines motion references and controller inputs offline to improve end-effector accuracy, producing robot-compatible stateaction supervision. We evaluate policies trained with this supervision on Unitree G1 across seven representative tasks spanning coordinated whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation (Sec. 5.1). Using task-specific human demonstrations without target-task robot demonstrations, the evaluations achieve mean progress of 51.7% and 76.2%, respectively. Using this capture setup, we build HUMANVERSE, 500-hour corpus of human loco-manipulation spanning open-world scenes and tasks. We record egocentric video and body motion with lightweight wearable sensors, synchronize the streams, and reconstruct hand motion from video. We develop λ0, whole-body humanoid visionlanguageaction policy that learns from scalable human experience and progressively adapts it to humanoid control  (Fig. 1)  . Egocentric hand-motion pretraining draws on diverse human interaction videos. Mid-training on HUMANVERSE then provides scalable, robot-free source of supervision for learning coordinated body and hand actions, bridging video pretraining and limited, costly robot demonstrations. Robot post-training adapts the learned behaviors to the target humanoid. Increasing whole-body human data reduces validation loss and raises real-world task progress monotonically from 59.9% without whole-body mid-training to 80.4% with the full corpus. Ablations identify whole-body mid-training as the larger contributor to real-world success among the two human-data stages. The full λ0 policy achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across four real-world locomanipulation tasks, improving over the strongest evaluated baselines by 3.9% and 22.5%, respectively. Human-data training also improves progress on robot-unseen object instances observed in human demonstrations. Our contributions are: We develop human-to-humanoid alignment pipeline for whole-body skill transfer and evaluate its collection efficiency and zero-shot transfer on G1 without target-task robot demonstrations. We introduce HUMANVERSE, 500-hour dataset pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion across open-world scenes and tasks. We develop λ0 to progressively adapt egocentric human interaction experience to humanoid control, and demonstrate that scaling human data with whole-body supervision improves downstream locomanipulation.

sections.title: 2.1 Generalist Robot Policies
sections.content: Large-scale robot datasets combine demonstrations across tasks and embodiments, supporting the development of generalist policies (Dasari et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2022; Walke et al., 2023; Open XEmbodiment Collaboration, 2024; Brohan et al., 2023; Zitkovich et al., 2023; Khazatsky et al., 2024; Bu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026b). These policies learn from diverse demonstrations within shared model (Ghosh et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2025), motivating more scalable ways to collect training data. Advances in teleoperation and portable demonstration interfaces reduce collection effort (Dass et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2025b; Chi et al., 2024). UMI on Legs extends robot-free hand-held demonstrations to quadruped manipulation by coupling task-level manipulation policy with simulation-trained whole-body controller (Ha et al., 2025). Robot-based collection depends on hardware availability and repeated resets, while portable interfaces have limited action spaces.

sections.title: 2.2 Learning from Human Videos
sections.content: Human video datasets capture diverse activities, objects, and environments, providing rich experience for robot learning (Grauman et al., 2022; Damen et al., 2022; Goyal et al., 2017; Grauman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023b; DeTone et al., 2026; Lightwheel AI, 2026). Learning from it requires connecting observations to actions. Nymeria pairs synchronized multimodal egocentric recordings with full-body motion across 300 hours of daily activities in the wild (Ma et al., 2024), providing foundation for studying contextdependent human motion. Temporal and geometric annotations describe when interactions occur and how hands and objects move (Liu et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025; Sener et al., 2022; Ragusa et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2024; Banerjee et al., 2025), while motion tracking and reconstruction provide human trajectories for action learning (Hoque et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026a). OpenEgo standardizes hand-pose annotations and temporally localized action descriptions across egocentric datasets (Jawaid & Xiang, 2025). Human videos also support visual representation learning (Nair et al., 2023; Sontakke et al., 2023; Kumar et al., 2020) and robot control through imitation and alignment (Mandlekar et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2020; Bahl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023a; Bharadhwaj et al., 2023; Kareer et al., 2025; Lepert et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026b). HAT unifies human and humanoid stateaction spaces for co-training on aligned PH2D demonstrations (Qiu et al., 2025), while DexWild combines wearable human interaction data with robot demonstrations for dexterous manipulation across environments (Tao et al., 2025). EgoZero learns closed-loop manipulation from smart-glasses demonstrations without robot data using morphology-agnostic representations (Liu et al., 2025), while HumanEgo uses handobject interaction representations to learn robot-data-free policies from short human recordings (Wang et al., 2026b). Beyond stationary manipulation, EMMA co-trains human full-body mobile manipulation demonstrations with static robot data, avoiding mobile robot teleoperation and reporting improved performance as human data increases (Zhu et al., 2026). We use synchronized body and hand motion as action supervision for bipedal humanoid loco-manipulation, and measure the benefit of increasing this data while holding robot demonstrations fixed. 2.3 Humanoid Whole-Body Control Humanoid whole-body control coordinates locomotion, posture, and manipulation to support complex physical interactions (Fu et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026b). Motion retargeting is key interface: GMR studies how retargeting artifacts affect downstream tracking (Araujo et al., 2026), and Human2Humanoid combines morphology-invariant trajectory alignment with physics-aware feasibility constraints (Huang et al., 2026). Humanoid policies learn task-level behaviors from human experience through latent video actions, geometric pretraining, or joint training on human and robot demonstrations (Jiang et al., 2026a; Wei et al., 2026b; Shi et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Bjorck et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026a). ZeroWBC generates and tracks whole-body motion from an initial egocentric image and language instruction without robot teleoperation demonstrations (Yang et al., 2026a); HALOMI couples egocentric demonstration capture with view alignment and controller-aware reference adaptation for active-perception loco-manipulation (Zhao et al., 2026a). Simulation provides another route from human video to control: VideoMimic reconstructs human motion and scenes for contextual control (Allshire et al., 2025), and SUGAR physically refines human-video interaction priors before distilling autonomous policies (Wu et al., 2026). GRAIL instead synthesizes interactions from 3D assets and video priors to train visual policies through simulation (Xie et al., 2026). LEGS combines procedurally generated demonstrations with photorealistic Gaussian-splatting scene backgrounds to fine-tune humanoid loco-manipulation VLAs without teleoperation (Kim et al., 2026). Predictive models and integrated whole-body systems offer complementary ways to connect perception, motion, and control (Li et al., 2026b; Symbiosis Robotics, 2026; Figure AI, 2026a; Parada, 2026; Zheng et al., 2026a; Ye et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). sections.title: 3 HumanVerse: Scaling Egocentric Whole-Body Data Collection in the Open World
sections.content: HUMANVERSE contains 500 hours of egocentric human loco-manipulation, comprising 32,993 episodes and 87 million pose frames  (Fig. 2)  . The dataset covers 827 task types across diverse objects and scenes, pairing first-person video with synchronized body and hand motion. We convert these recordings into robot-aligned whole-body human data for training; the 500-hour figure describes the recorded human corpus before conversion and validity filtering. 3.1 Data Collection Setup and Protocol We choose the GoPro HERO13 for convenient human data collection and equip our downstream robot, Unitree G1, with the same camera on its head. We align the human camera height with the robot camera using neck mount, while PICO 4 Ultra headset and body trackers capture body motion alongside the video. We reconstruct hand motion from the same video. Figure 3 summarizes the workflow from open-world scene and task selection to robot-free capture, data curation, and robot alignment. Figure 3: Robot-free capture, curation, and robot alignment. We select open-world scenes and tasks and record egocentric video, body motion, and speech with robot-matched camera viewpoint. Curation includes synchronization, language/task annotation, body and hand motion reconstruction, observation alignment, action alignment, and quality inspection. Modality thumbnails are schematic. Collection protocol. Collectors receive activity-level prompts rather than prescribed joint trajectories, allowing variation in walking paths, initial posture, object instances, placements, grasp strategies, and intermediate corrections. Each episode preserves the approach, repositioning, and transitions needed to complete an interaction, rather than only the final hand motion. Collectors use the wearable interface in everyday locations without an on-site robot, focusing on carrying, tidying, cleaning, and operating objects and fixtures. We retain original streams, collector and session identifiers, activity labels, calibration, and device-health records. On-site checks flag interruptions, missing modalities, and calibration failures.

sections.title: 3.2 Dataset Scope and Coverage
sections.content: HUMANVERSE denotes only the 500-hour synchronized egocentric whole-body corpus. External hand object datasets and robot demonstrations are excluded from its duration and scaling subsets; their training roles are described in Sec. 4.2. HUMANVERSE captures everyday activities in homes, retail and supermarket spaces, industrial sites, offices, and outdoor areas. Activities include cleaning, cooking, personal care, laundry, table setting, and large-object transport. For example, interacting with objects at different heights involves bending or reaching, while transporting objects couples walking with sustained grasping. Figure 2 summarizes the task, scene, object, and motion distributions, while Supplementary Table 4 compares the datasets capture setup and motion coverage with existing egocentric datasets. Qualitative task diversity. Figure 4 presents 60 egocentric frames illustrating everyday tasks, scenes, and manipulated objects. Each tile depicts one moment from capture session. These examples illustrate qualitative diversity and do not estimate dataset-wide task frequencies. Figure 4: Representative examples from HUMANVERSE. Sixty first-person frames are arranged in 12 5 gallery to illustrate diversity in tasks, scenes, objects, and handobject interactions. 3.3 Human Motion Reconstruction and Annotation Temporal synchronization and language annotation. The GoPro and PICO run on independent clocks. We assign each episode time offset under the convention tpico = tgopro + and refine capture-time prior by cross-correlating GoPro gyroscope measurements with tracker-derived body angular velocity. After applying this offset, video and body pose are resampled onto common timeline over their overlapping interval, with synchronization quality retained as an explicit diagnostic. Spoken instructions on the GoPro audio track are transcribed into episode-level language/task labels. The records retain stable frame indices for reconstruction and alignment. Body and hand motion. We reconstruct synchronized human motion sequence from wearable body tracking and egocentric video. The PICO system (PICO, n.d.) supplies timestamped 24-joint body kinematics, while Dyn-HaMR (Yu et al., 2025) estimates 21 joints per hand using camera motion from ViPE (Huang et al., 2025). Coordinate transforms register these trajectories to the synchronized video frames. These body and hand trajectories provide the reference for robot alignment in Sec. 3.4. Coordinate representations. We retain the camera trajectory and available camera-to-world and bodyframe transforms. Hand trajectories are stored both in current-camera coordinates for reprojection and in an episode-fixed frame anchored at the first valid camera pose to preserve displacement over time. Finger geometry is represented in wrist-local, palm-aligned, scale-normalized coordinates. Annotation records. Each derived motion sequence retains source-frame indices, coordinate transforms, conversion versions, per-track visibility, and estimator confidence. Raw recordings are the canonical source. Separate body and hand validity masks preserve usable body motion when hands are missing or occluded, without interpolating missing poses. The body stream consists of wearable-device kinematics; the hand trajectories are reconstructed from RGB. Validation and splits are detailed in Appendix C. Figure 5: Synchronized human motion and egocentric observations. Top: egocentric RGB frames. Bottom: corresponding SMPL body meshes with MANO hand motion and illustrative camera frusta. Camera frusta schematically illustrate viewing direction. Data quality and splits. We partition HUMANVERSE by recording session before extracting temporal windows and draw nested scaling subsets only from the frozen general-purpose training partition. Task-specific human demonstrations for downstream post-training remain separate from this corpus, and human-data selection does not consult the humanoid evaluation manifest. Appendix details the quality checks, validity masking, and split protocol. Figure 5 shows 16 examples pairing egocentric frames with their reconstructed motions. 3.4 Human-to-Humanoid Alignment Pipeline We align the recorded images and reconstructed motions to G1  (Fig. 3)  . Observation alignment matches camera settings and replaces human arms with rendered robot arms. Action alignment refines motion references and controller inputs offline, producing humanoid states and motion tokens in the action interface used at deployment. Action Alignment. Humanoids rely on tracking policy such as SONIC (Luo et al., 2026b) for coordinated whole-body loco-manipulation. Motion references obtained through retargeting, such as GMR (Araujo et al., 2026), or human-motion execution through SONIC can still yield end-effector pose errors. Geometric mismatch affects the reference, while controller tracking introduces additional exeFigure 6: Human-to-humanoid action alignment. The first two stages modify the human and robot references. The third accounts for execution dynamics and directly optimizes motion tokens using gradient-based updates. End-effector targets remain fixed throughout. Rendered poses illustrate the procedure and are not experimental rollouts. 7 cution error. These errors can compromise grasping and contact. We refine the human reference, robot reference, and controller inputs offline in three stages  (Fig. 6)  (Jiang et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026). (1) Human-reference alignment: Height differences between the human reference and G1 can shift end effectors away from the targets. We scale SMPL copy to G1 height, adjust its pose to align end effectors with the fixed targets, and apply these corrections to the human reference. SONIC rollout yields better-aligned G1 motion. (2) Robot-reference alignment: The scaled SMPL skeleton still differs from G1s body geometry, leaving residual end-effector errors. We correct the robot reference through constrained offline whole-body inverse kinematics (IK) using G1s kinematic model. Re-encoding the corrected reference and replaying its tokens further reduces these errors. (3) Dynamics-aware optimization: Execution dynamics introduce errors that kinematic correction alone cannot resolve. We use rollout feedback and response model to guide gradient-based updates to the motion tokens. Multiple rounds of token updates and rollouts progressively reduce end-effector errors. During dataset production, we select the best valid result across the three stages. SONIC rollout of the original human poses serves as fallback if alignment yields no improvement. We validate the latter two stages on 50 tasks (about 1 of data), reducing task-averaged end-effector errors from 17.03 to 3.83 cm in position and from 36.06 to 10.85 in orientation. Observation Alignment. We use the same camera model and match capture height to reduce viewpoint differences between human and robot recordings. To align arm appearance, we mask human forearms and wrist-mounted PICO trackers with SAM2 (Ravi et al., 2025) and inpaint these regions with DiffuEraser (Li et al., 2025). We then render G1 arms from the aligned joint positions, fit them to the human wrists and forearms, and composite them onto the inpainted frames. This preserves the scene and interaction. Human and humanoid motion can still alter camera viewpoints. During training, random resized crops, small rotations, and photometric jitter improve robustness to these differences. The deployed policy uses humanoid images. 4 λ0: Learning Humanoid Loco-manipulation from Human Experience λ0 uses visionlanguageaction architecture and domain-specific interfaces to learn task-conditioned actions from human experience. sections.content: We evaluate whether the human-supervised training recipe improves humanoid loco-manipulation across simulation and real-world tasks by comparing λ0 with established policy baselines. Figure 10: Real-world data collection and evaluation. (a) Egocentric teleoperation collects whole-body demonstrations. (b) Four loco-manipulation tasks evaluate task success. (c) Robot-seen and robot-unseen objects are used for standard task and generalization evaluation, respectively. Hardware. PICO 4 Ultra with five trackers captures body motion, which SONIC converts into Unitree G1 control signals (Fig. 10(a)). sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented λ0, foundation model for humanoid loco-manipulation, and HUMANVERSE, an egocentric whole-body human dataset that supports learning from open-world interaction without robot-operated collection. Human-to-humanoid alignment makes this experience usable for learning coordinated body and hand actions. Whole-body human mid-training bridges diverse human interaction videos and limited, costly robot demonstrations, progressively extending hand-motion pretraining to whole-body control before adaptation to the target humanoid. Our results show that scaling this human supervision improves downstream loco-manipulation, supporting egocentric whole-body human experience as practical source of data for humanoid learning.

sections.title: C Data Quality and Scaling Protocol
sections.content: Data quality. frozen episode manifest records provenance, capture metadata, annotation coverage, conversion versions, and split assignments. Structural checks verify timestamps, stream overlap and lengths, coordinate conventions, and finite valid values. Hand reprojection into RGB and synchronized visual inspection assess geometric consistency. Invalid targets are masked, and reconstruction diagnostics and conversion failures are retained. Dataset summaries cover corpus size and diversity, annotation coverage, and conversion failures; visual checks provide qualitative reconstruction diagnostics. Data splits and validation. We partition HUMANVERSE by recording session before extracting temporal windows, so all windows from an episode inherit the same split. Task-specific human demonstrations collected for downstream post-training remain separate from the general-purpose mid-training corpus. Session, object-instance, and evaluation-configuration identifiers track experimental separation; humandata selection does not consult the robot evaluation manifest. Clean contains held-out sessions whose frame-weighted validity ratios for both SONIC whole-body and bilateral hand annotations reach their respective upper-quartile thresholds in the original split. Here, clean refers to annotation validity rather than appearance or task difficulty. Representative is stratified by data source and quartile bins of the two validity ratios. The sets contain 1,008 and 513 episodes, respectively, each from 44 capture sessions. Their sessions are mutually disjoint and excluded from training; both sets remain fixed across data fractions. Scaling protocol. The human-data scaling axis is expressed as fraction of the frozen HUMANVERSE training partition, with validation sessions excluded before subset construction. The 0%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% conditions define the evaluation grid for Fig. 12. Nonzero subsets are nested, sampled at the episode level, and stratified by activity and recording session before chunk extraction. The Stage-I checkpoint, robot post-training set, Stage-III update budget, validation sets, and evaluation manifest remain fixed. The primary compute-matched comparison uses the same number of Stage-II optimizer updates for every nonzero fraction; the 0% reference omits Stage II. Fig. 11 reports the 2B model at the five nonzero fractions, each trained for 100k updates with seed 43. Total validation loss is evaluated every 1k updates with validation seed 20260813.
